Abstract
This work addresses the challenges associated with reactive transport modeling in environmental
applications, such as nuclear waste disposal and geological sequestration of CO2. Due to limited expe-
rimental studies in long-term scenarios, numerical simulation is crucial. A thorough survey of existing
codes reveals mainly two types of numerical approaches for reactive ﬂows : global implicit and sequential
or operator splitting approaches. Sequential approaches allow speciﬁc programming for hydrological and
chemical processes. The objective is to develop a reactive transport package that couples PHREEQC for
chemical aspects and DuMuX for hydrological aspects. The operator splitting method is implemented in
a non-iterative sequential approach and a comprehensive description of the mathematical formulation is
presented. The spatial discretization employs a cell-centered ﬁnite volume method with an implicit Euler
scheme for time discretization. The model has been developed and implemented for both single-phase
and two-phase ﬂows. Its efﬁciency and robustness have been validated through a series of numerical ex-
periments, ranging from single-phase benchmarks to complex two-phase ﬂow scenarios. The methodo-
logy has been tested notably in two- and three-dimensional conﬁgurations, including high-performance
computing, thereby demonstrating its relevance for realistic applications.
Keywords : Reactive transport, Multiphase ﬂow, Sequential coupling, DuMuX, PHREEQC

Introduction
Reactive transport plays a crucial role in various environmental applications, including nuclear waste
disposal [11] and geological sequestration of CO2 [43]. In such long-term applications, experimental
studies are limited, and numerical modeling becomes an essential tool for understanding the fate of
chemical species and conducting predictive studies [51]. A comprehensive review of existing codes
for reactive transport modeling can be found in [55, 69]. Among these codes, we can mention, wi-
thout being exhaustive, IPARS [61], PFLOTRAN [27], NUFT [28], TOUGHREACT [65], HYTEC [58],
eSTOMP [62], MIN3P [39], HYDROGEOCHEM [66], OpenGeoSys [33], ADGPRS [24], CORE2D
V4 [49], PROOST [25], DARTS [59] or Reaktoro [35]. Despite ongoing efforts to develop new me-
thods and algorithms for reactive transport modeling, numerical modeling of this phenomenon remains
challenging. Challenges arise from the fact that both the chemical and physical aspects of the reactive
transport process consist of coupled processes occurring at different temporal and spatial scales. The
difﬁculty is further compounded by coupling the hydrological and chemical sides [54, 12]. To address
such coupled processes, two approaches for solving reactive transport problems are mainly found in the
literature [67]. The Global Implicit Approach (GIA) solves a unique system that combines chemical

reactions governed by mass action laws or ordinary differential equations and ﬂow governed by mass
conservation laws. The sequential approach, also known as the operator splitting approach, decouples
the hydrological and chemical sides of reactive transport and has been widely reported in the literature
(see, for example, [16, 34, 37, 57]). Moreover, the operator splitting method facilitates the adoption of
a modular structure in programming reactive transport models, providing signiﬁcant convenience for
integrating diverse physical and chemical processes. This approach enables the implementation of dedi-
cated modules for each hydrological and chemical aspect, optimizing the utilization of codes speciﬁcally
designed for the chemical and hydrological sides of reactive transport. It can also help mitigate the nu-
merical diffusion commonly introduced by implicit schemes, which can limit the accuracy of Global
Implicit Approaches (GIA), especially in applications with high Péclet numbers and when SNIA is com-
bined with high-resolution spatial discretizations [18]. A growing trend in the literature highlights the
external coupling of such codes and the development of new reactive transport packages. For example,
HYTEC, structured modularly, utilizes the geochemical module CHESS on the chemical side [58]. In
many other works, the external geochemical package PHREEQC [44] is employed for coupling with
ﬂow and transport codes. For instance, Šim˘unek et al [50] developed HPx by coupling PHREEQC with
HYDRUS1. PHAST [45] and PHT3D[47, 63] couples PHREEQC with HST3D and MT3DMS for ﬂow
and transport calculations, respectively. In [30], the authors describe the integration of the open-source
software OpenGeoSys with PHREEQC. PHREEQC has also been extensively coupled with COMSOL
Multiphysics [15]. Beyond Wissmeier’s pioneering work on PHREEQC-COMSOL coupling [60], we
can mention, non exhaustively, the iCP framework [42], where Nardi et al. coupled PHREEQC with a
variably saturated, non-isothermal reactive transport model. Additionally, in [31], a new object-oriented
platform was developed to facilitate the coupling of PHREEQC and COMSOL, while [26] presents
a COMSOL-PHREEQC interface to simulate reactive transport for cement-based materials. Recently,
PHREEQC has been successfully coupled with the open-source software OpenFOAM in continuum/pore
scale [52]. In [8], PHREEQC was also combined with OpenFOAM to transfer and expand the capabilities
of the MODFLOW/MT3DMS-family of codes. In the aforementioned works, the motivation for coupling
PHREEQC with specialized transport codes lies in the capability of PHREEQC to recognize a variety
of instantaneous and kinetic reactions simply via basic scripts, enabling a ﬂexible deﬁnition of chemical
formulations [70]. Furthermore, the efforts of PHREEQC developers have led to the development of a
reactive transport module PhreeqcRM that makes the coupling between PHREEQC and transport simu-
lators using an operator-splitting approach more convenient [46]. PhreeqcRM has been extensively used
to integrate geochemical models into hydrological codes, offering signiﬁcant ﬂexibility in accessing the
full range of PHREEQC’s reaction capabilities. In [38], PhreeqcRM was coupled with SUTRA-MS [29],
a variable-saturation and variable-density multi-component solute transport model. Similarly, in [68],
it was integrated with IC-FERST (Imperial College Finite Element Reservoir Simulator). Additionally,
PhreeqcRM has been employed to train machine learning surrogate models for predicting the evolution
of complex subsurface systems [53]. Notably, it has also been linked with hydrological models in [40]
and [41].
For the hydrological side, the capability of the model for a comprehensive and efﬁcient representation
of the system is a vital point. Among robust physical models, DuMuX is a free and open-source simulator
specialized for modeling ﬂow and transport processes in porous media [32]. It is based on the DUNE
parallel library [9, 10], allowing high-performance calculations. Over the past decade, we have actively
contributed to the development of DuMuX by implementing a variety of numerical schemes dedicated
to reactive transport modeling. Notably, a series of works [7, 5, 3] introduced a sequential strategy that
decomposes the global problem into two subproblems : a two-phase compositional ﬂow followed by a
reactive transport problem, enabling a modular and ﬂexible solution framework. In [7, 5], the reactive
transport step was tackled using a sequential iterative approach (SIA), which iteratively couples transport
2


and chemistry. However, in order to reduce time-splitting errors inherent to the SIA framework, a fully
implicit approach was introduced in [3], treating ﬂow and reactive transport in a more tightly integrated
manner. Building on this foundation, a fully implicit and fully coupled method was later developed,
based on a direct substitution approach, as described in [4, 6]. The fully implicit approach, which solves
ﬂow and chemical interactions within a single nonlinear system, can improve stability and coupling for
highly coupled problems. The implicit strategy has been thoroughly validated, notably through recent
benchmark studies in the ﬁelds of CO2 sequestration [2] and nuclear waste disposal [48]. Recently, these
methodologies have been further extended to model coupled Thermo-Hydro-Chemical (THC) processes,
supporting both fully implicit and sequential formulations [1], thus broadening the applicability of the
framework to a wider range of complex scenarios. Most of the previous developments were constrained
by the limited complexity of the chemical system, often relying on simpliﬁed assumptions such as an
ideal activity model. Therefore, the objective of this work is to develop a new reactive transport package
that integrates the advantages of DuMuX on the hydrological side with the wide range of advantages of
PHREEQC for the chemical side.
An operator splitting approach has been implemented using a non-iterative sequential approach. The-
refore, the challenges in each subproblem are handled by a code specialized for that subproblem. On the
hydrological side, the system consists of Darcy’s law for each ﬂuid phase, coupled with mass conser-
vation laws and some closure relations. In each time step, the system is coupled with the chemical side
through the dependence of reaction rates on the species concentrations. With a wide range of values
for the reaction rates, including fast equilibrium reactions and slow kinetic reactions, the full system
becomes quite stiff [23]. A classical way to deal with the stiffness of the system is to remove the fast
equilibrium rates from mass conservation by deﬁning primary and secondary species and writing the
mass conservation equations based on the total (general) concentration of primary species. The system
is then closed based on ordinary differential equations or mass action law written for each chemical
reaction [36]. This approach, also known as the primary species-based approach, requires the deﬁnition
of all primary and secondary species in the physical system to obtain mass conservation based on total
concentration, which depends on both primary and secondary species. With a large number of species
in a realistic reactive transport model, the programming efforts to account for all these species become
enormous. To overcome this challenge, in this work, we implemented an element-based approach, which
writes the mass conservation laws based on element concentrations [22, 24]. An element is deﬁned as
an atom or a compound that remains chemically indivisible within the considered system. This method,
introduced for the ﬁrst time in DuMuX, involves applying a linear transformation to the system of mass
conservation equations for each species.
The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the formulation of the reactive
two-phase ﬂow problem. It presents the mathematical model and provides a detailed description of the
sequential scheme used to decouple the original problem into two subproblems. Section 3 focuses on the
numerical implementation of these subproblems using two software tools : DuMuX for the hydrologi-
cal component and PHREEQC for the geochemical processes. Finally, Section 4 presents the numerical
results, divided into two subsections. The ﬁrst addresses the single-phase ﬂow case and includes a compa-
rison with one-dimensional computations performed using standalone PHREEQC. The second presents
applications involving two-phase ﬂow and discusses two- and three-dimensional numerical experiments,
including High Performance Computing aspects.

2.2
Solving strategy
In accordance with the methodology presented in [3, 5], we propose to use a sequential approach
that divides the original problem composed of equations (10), mass action laws and ordinary differential
equations into two distinct subproblems. The initial subproblem focuses on computing an implicit two-
phase compositional ﬂow, taking into consideration only the species present in both liquid and gas phases

(for instance H2O and CO2 in scenario of geological storage of CO2). During this step, exchanges bet-
ween phases are comprehensively resolved, while the contribution of other species is explicitly addressed
or neglected. In the subsequent subproblem, a reactive single-phase transport problem is solved using the
ﬂow properties obtained from the preceding two-phase ﬂow step (liquid phase’s saturation, density, and
velocity, etc). This second step focuses on the transport and geochemical evolution of species that were
treated explicitly in the two-phase ﬂow computation, including dissolved ions, sorbed species, and mine-
ral phases. Additionally, this step potentially allows for the dynamic update of porosity and permeability
in response to mineral reactions, thereby capturing feedbacks between geochemistry and ﬂow properties.

Numerical implementation
In this section, we describe the dedicated numerical codes designed to solve each subproblem and
explain the coupling mechanisms employed within each module. The hydrological component is imple-
mented in DuMuX, using a cell-centered ﬁnite volume (FV) method to solve compositional two-phase
ﬂow and transport equations with implicit time integration. The geochemical processes are modeled
using PHREEQC, which offers ﬂexible handling of both equilibrium and kinetic reactions. These two
components are coupled through a sequential operator-splitting approach, where DuMuX computes ﬂow
and non-reactive transport, and PHREEQC, via PhreeqcRM, performs geochemical calculations based
on the transported concentrations.
3.1
Hydrological model : DuMuX
The resolution of both the compositional two-phase ﬂow subproblem (11) and the transport step of
the reactive transport subproblem (20) has been fully implemented in DuMuX [32]. The modular de-
sign of DuMuX facilitates the straightforward incorporation of a wide range of constitutive relations,
enabling a comprehensive integration of diverse physical processes. The compositional two-phase ﬂow
subproblem is governed by Darcy’s law for each phase, along with mass conservation laws for species
distributed across both the liquid and gas phases. These are supplemented by constitutive and thermo-
dynamic closure relations, including capillary pressure-saturation relationships, phase equilibrium ex-
pressed through fugacity equality, and equations of state for ﬂuid properties. The transport step involves

3.3
Coupling DuMuX and PHREEQC
The detailed coupling strategy is shown in Figure 1. The algorithm is based on a sequential operator-
splitting approach to solve the coupled problem of compositional two-phase ﬂow and reactive transport.
The two-phase ﬂow subproblem is ﬁrst solved using DuMuX. The output variables for the liquid, such
as saturation, velocity, density and concentrations of species present in both phases, are passed to the
reactive transport module. This reactive transport step is divided into two parts. In the transport step,
DuMuX solves the mass conservation equations for chemical elements under the assumption of non-
reactive transport. The resulting concentrations are then used as input to the geochemical step, which
is handled by PHREEQC. Speciﬁcally, PhreeqcRM [46], which maintains the full functionality of the
reaction capabilities of PHREEQC, is called in each time step after transport calculations for geochemical
calculations. As input to the PhreeqcRM class, the total mobile concentrations of elements for every
cell discretizing the physical domain are written in an array given to PhreeqcRM. This step accounts
for local chemical reactions, including equilibrium and kinetic processes, by solving a set of nonlinear
algebraic and differential equations that ensure mass conservation and reaction balance. The updated
values, namely the liquid-phase concentrations Cl,updated

of species shared between two phases, as well
as the explicit revision of porosity and permeability, are then provided to the two-phase ﬂow module to
initialize the next time step.

Conclusions and perspectives
This work details the development of a reactive transport package coupling the advantages of DuMuX
for hydrological processes with the capabilities of PHREEQC for chemical reactions. The operator split-
ting approach, through a sequential non-iterative approach, is implemented to handle the coupling bet-
ween the two subproblems efﬁciently. Before applying this methodology to two-phase ﬂow, the coupling
DuMuX-PHREEQC was validated on reactive single-phase ﬂow through two test cases. The ﬁrst test
involved a calcite dissolution problem while the second one focused on inﬁltration process in a granitic
bedrock. The results from both test cases were in good agreement with reference solutions obtained using
PHREEQC alone. To further evaluate the capability of the methodology in modeling reactive two-phase
ﬂow, two comprehensive test cases were conducted. The ﬁrst test concerns a two-dimensional benchmark
for geological storage of CO2, and the results showed good agreement with a fully implicit approach.
The second test case addresses geological CO2 storage in a heterogeneous three-dimensional geometry,
incorporating high-performance simulations. It demonstrates the capabilities of our sequential coupling
in handling realistic scenarios.
Consequently, the reactive transport developed in this work provides a versatile tool for studying
complex environmental scenarios involving coupled hydrological and chemical processes. The ﬂexibility
of PHREEQC for chemical calculations, combined with the efﬁciency of the simulator DuMuX to solve
transport and multiphase ﬂows, through an operator splitting strategy, makes the proposed methodology
a valuable contribution to the ﬁeld of reactive transport modeling. Compared to previous developments in
reactive transport modeling within DuMuX, this approach offers greater ﬂexibility for addressing more
complex chemical scenarios and exploring new applications, such as hydrogen geological storage or
geothermal energy. Finally, the comprehensive description of the coupling algorithm employed in the
element-based formulation simpliﬁes the integration of any reservoir simulator with PHREEQC, enhan-
cing versatility and ease of implementation.

Abstract: This work addresses the challenges associated with reactive transport modeling in environmental applications, such as nuclear waste disposal and geological sequestration of CO2. Due to limited expe- rimental studies in long-term scenarios, numerical simulation is crucial. A thorough survey of existing codes reveals mainly two types of numerical approaches for reactive ﬂows : global implicit and sequential or operator splitting approaches. Sequential approaches allow speciﬁc programming for hydrological and chemical processes. The objective is to develop a reactive transport package that couples PHREEQC for chemical aspects and DuMuX for hydrological aspects. The operator splitting method is implemented in a non-iterative sequential approach and a comprehensive description of the mathematical formulation is presented. The spatial discretization employs a cell-centered ﬁnite volume method with an implicit Euler scheme for time discretization. The model has been developed and implemented for both single-phase and two-phase ﬂows. Its efﬁciency and robustness have been validated through a series of numerical ex- periments, ranging from single-phase benchmarks to complex two-phase ﬂow scenarios. The methodo- logy has been tested notably in two- and three-dimensional conﬁgurations, including high-performance computing, thereby demonstrating its relevance for realistic applications.
